heading: Background and foreground
body:
`ApplicationStateChanged` tells a service that the app went to the background or came back to the foreground. It has one field, `state`, and its value is `background` or `foreground`. Use it to pause work that nobody can see, such as a timer or a stream, and to start the work again later.

| Where the page runs | `background` | `foreground` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Browser tab | The tab is hidden. | The tab is shown again. |
| macOS app | The app stops being the active app, the app is hidden, or its window is minimized. | The app is the active app again and its window is shown. |
| Windows app | The app is no longer the active app (`WM_ACTIVATEAPP`), or its window is minimized. | The app is the active app again, or its window is restored. |
| Linux app | No window of the app is active, or the window is suspended. | A window of the app is active again. |
| iOS app | The app enters the background (`didEnterBackground`). | The app comes back (`willEnterForeground`). |
| Android app | The activity stops (`onStop`). | The activity starts again (`onStart`). |

In a browser tab, the page sends the event when the page visibility changes. In a desktop or mobile app, the native host sends it, and the page does not use its visibility for it.

The event model is built in: do not declare it in `client/models/`. Write a listener with a parameter of type `ApplicationStateChanged`, like any `@OnEvent` listener. The page publishes the current state when it starts and keeps it, so a listener with `replay` hears the current state first and then every change. The event needs no permission and no browser API field, so a Python service can listen to it too, although Python services have no browser APIs.

A service that is linked into a desktop or mobile app (Swift, Kotlin, C# and Rust; see \"What a native service reaches\") can listen to `ApplicationStateChanged` too. It is the one built-in event model that the build does not refuse in a linked service (`TY1317`).

In a desktop or mobile app, a page script that is not a service can also listen to the DOM event `tac.application.state` on `window`. The new state is in `event.detail.state`.
